source.title: (tentatively) Found 600+ Monosemantic Features in a Small LM Using Sparse Autoencoders

record.file_problem: Whole post and comments are present. Some referenced graphs and linked spreadsheet are not reproduced in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Reports sparse-autoencoder features in a language model, extending feature-recovery evidence to an LLM setting rather than reproducing the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The post tests whether a sparse autoencoder yields interpretable, cross-dictionary features and whether those features involve multiple neurons. The cited prior work and the linked spreadsheet are not treated as this study's results. The 500k-token search is a selection procedure, not a result row.
record.test_reason: Trains sparse autoencoders on Pythia-70M layer-2 mid-MLP activations. It reports a sparse, interpretable feature spread over many neurons (V4) and compares features across separately trained dictionaries (V5 stability). This is an LLM setting, not the original toy-model method.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author claims 'pretty strong evidence' that the dictionary yields meaningful features that are linear combinations of neurons, not monosemantic neurons. He also notes that he chose a feature representing a polysemantic neuron. He calls the results tentative, finding 600+ features but expecting 8k-16k. He lists open work on coverage, low-MCS features, cross-layer connections and metrics.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse autoencoders and cross-dictionary comparisons on Pythia-70M activations, rather than the original toy-network setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature interpretation and apparent consistency vary with MCS; many lower-MCS features were inactive or not checked. The number of neurons attributed to the example feature also depends on the activation threshold.
record.problems: One model and layer; the post describes the evidence as preliminary. Many low-MCS features were dead or not examined, numerical summaries for the feature survey are not provided here, and some conclusions depend on informal interpretation of activations and neuron thresholds.
record.rows_left_out: The post mentions a quick check of the top 70 MCS features but gives no aggregate result in the text. Other mentioned figures and the linked spreadsheet are not sufficiently described to extract additional separate outcomes.

untested.parts: No toy model, no sparsity-dependent transition, no geometry.
No test of capacity competition or feature importance.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Completeness is only the author's expectation (600+ found vs 8k-16k expected) and is not measured. Canonicality is not systematically measured.
No comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features.
Only one model and one layer. Only one feature is studied in depth. The top-70 survey is not summarised in the text.

missing.what: Headline count: 600+ features judged learned, against 8k-16k the author expects to be learnable. This bears on V5 completeness, but the expected figure is the author's estimate.
Neuron-activation graph across the top-50 high-MCS features in the main dictionary. Its result is not stated in the text.
Identity-dictionary feature drops to 1 neuron above threshold 0.8, with only 1 weight >0.04 (2.9). The author uses this as a contrast supporting about 60 neurons for feature #52.

record.verdict_notes: I removed the record's V5 'challenges' label. The 8k-16k figure is the author's expectation, not a measured result, and is not in any row. A LessWrong post with no peer review. Figures and the spreadsheet are not reproduced in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network test of feature overlap, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test capacity competition, feature importance, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
One model and one layer are studied; this is not a broad survey of models or a systematic measure of how features are distributed across neurons.
Does not establish completeness, stability across training choices or datasets, or canonical status beyond the reported dictionary comparisons.
Uses decoder feature vectors, but does not compare one-dimensional directions against multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared feature vectors across two separately trained dictionaries using maximum cosine similarity (MCS).
rows.measure: Maximum cosine similarity between dictionary feature vectors
rows.locator: Feature Case Study; Top-activating Examples for feature #52
rows.note: The author treats the high similarity across separately trained dictionaries as evidence that the feature recurs.
rows.check: MCS ~0.99 is the criterion used to pick feature #52 for the case study, so it is a selection value, not a result. It cannot show stability across dictionaries in general.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Removed context tokens individually and measured the feature magnitude at the final position.

conditions.value: removing the final "$" makes the new final token "all"

rows.measure: Feature magnitude at the final position
rows.note: The post describes the feature as sparse and interprets it as detecting LaTeX dollar signs.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Removed context tokens individually and measured the feature magnitude at the final position.
rows.measure: Feature magnitude at the final position
rows.note: The author also says removing "where/let/for" affects activation; no separate values are stated for those contexts.
rows.check: The drop from 5 to 3.5 fits the LaTeX-$ interpretation the post proposes. 'Partial' misreads it as a weak effect relative to the version.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Subtracted the feature direction multiplied by its magnitude from the neuron activation, then examined output-logit changes.
rows.value: The post says effects appear limited to LaTeX-related tokens and can increase or decrease their log-probability; numerical values not stated.
rows.locator: Feature Case Study; Ablate Feature Direction
rows.note: The post notes that positions before the first feature activation are unaffected because the magnitude there is zero.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Inspected examples across bins of feature activation.
rows.measure: Semantic consistency of examples across feature activation levels
rows.value: The author says examples appear mainly related to LaTeX; an example involving "$ 100 billion tariff" has activation .14.
rows.note: The author raises the possibility that the feature responds to both mathematical and money-related uses of "$".

source_check.correct: state: observed for V4. Examples across activation bins appear mainly LaTeX-related; the money-related example activates at 0.14. V4 does not require perfect monosemanticity.
source_check.problem: The partial state treats uncertainty about strict monosemanticity as incomplete evidence for V4's weaker recoverability claim.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Prepended tokens to "for all $" and compared the resulting feature activations.
rows.value: Most-increasing tokens were described as ending-LaTeX-dollar related; most-decreasing tokens were described as more related to the money sense of "$"; the decreasing set numbered 97.
rows.note: The author says the interpretation fits the observed token changes but is not fully sure what all of the increasing tokens represent.
rows.check: The author says the prepended-token results fit the hypothesis. The uncertainty about some increasing tokens is minor.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Counted neurons exceeding activation thresholds across the top-10 examples for the feature.
rows.measure: Number of neurons above the stated activation threshold
rows.note: The post says many neurons exceeded zero, then reports 3 at threshold 0.5.

source_check.locator_found: Comparing to the Neuron Basis, lines 87–89

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Counted neurons whose activations exceeded neuron-specific quantile thresholds across the top-10 examples.
rows.measure: Number of neurons above the neuron-specific threshold
rows.note: The author says the appropriate threshold remains unclear.

source_check.locator_found: Comparing to the Neuron Basis, lines 87–91

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Examined the feature vector's neuron weights, scaled by the feature's maximum activation.
rows.measure: Estimated number of neurons affected by the feature vector
rows.value: The author estimates somewhere between 3 and 80 neurons, possibly several hundred depending on interpretation.
rows.note: This is explicitly presented as a rough estimate rather than a settled count.
rows.check: Every estimate (3 to 80, possibly hundreds) has the feature spread over more than one neuron, which is what V4 says. The imprecision is in the count, not the effect.

source_check.locator_found: Comparing to the Neuron Basis, lines 93–95

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared features from a different dictionary described as having learned the identity, using feature-neuron activation correlations.

conditions.value: different dictionary, described as the neuron basis

rows.measure: Number of neuron activations correlated with each feature
rows.value: The vast majority of features were said to correlate with only one neuron activation.
rows.note: The post does not state a numerical proportion, and the comparison is to the identity-like dictionary rather than the main feature dictionary.
rows.check: This is a control: an identity-like dictionary that recovers the neuron basis. It does not measure V4 itself. It contrasts with the main dictionary's high-MCS features, whose own graph is not reproduced.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the lower-MCS features in a comparison of separately trained dictionaries.
rows.measure: Feature activity and apparent semantic interpretability across dictionaries
rows.value: The author reports a trend that lower-MCS features appear more polysemantic; most were not checked because they were dead, with fewer than 10 activations and usually 0. The author later found more meaningful low-MCS features after training other dictionaries, including features found in one dictionary but not another.
rows.note: The post says it will provide a better statistic later; the reported comparison is qualitative.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Applied the logit lens to the dollar-sign feature and the 10 highest-MCS features.

conditions.value: the "$" feature and first 10 highest-MCS features

rows.measure: Whether the logit lens yielded meaningful features
rows.value: The author reports no meaningful features.
rows.note: This is a stated failure of the logit-lens analysis, not evidence that the autoencoder features themselves are absent.
rows.check: A logit-lens failure concerns how the feature's output effects can be read. It does not bear on whether sparse features are recovered or are canonical.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Examined the maximum logit difference when ablating the feature direction.
rows.measure: Tokens with the maximum logit difference under feature-direction ablation
rows.value: The author reports that the tokens were nonsense.
rows.note: The post characterizes this analysis as a failure to identify a meaningful feature.
rows.check: Nonsense tokens at the maximum logit difference reflect a failed interpretive tool. They are not a measure of the version.

relationships.reason: The SAE feature is sparse and interpretable under context ablation, uniform sampling and created examples. It spans 3 to 60+ neurons, unlike the identity dictionary (r2-r9).
relationships.display_finding: The feature stayed sparse and interpretable under context ablation, uniform sampling and constructed examples, and it spanned 3 to 60+ neurons, unlike the identity dictionary.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pythia-70M layer_2 mid-MLP after the GeLU; the dollar-sign feature and its neuron-basis comparisons
reader_labels.reason: The post reports an interpretable sparse feature and estimates that it involves multiple neurons, including a 60-neuron quantile-threshold count (r1-r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Lower-MCS features and the reported feature-interpretation checks
reader_labels.reason: Lower-MCS features were often inactive or appeared more polysemantic, and the post reports failures of two interpretive checks (r11-r13).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: High-MCS and lower-MCS features in separately trained dictionaries
reader_labels.reason: Feature #52 had high cross-dictionary similarity, but the post also reports low-MCS features that were inactive or not recovered in another dictionary; it does not establish a complete, canonical feature set (r1, r11).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Coverage of features in the studied layer
reader_labels.reason: The author reports finding 600+ features while expecting around 8k-16k learnable features, which does not support the claim that the learned dictionary is complete (r11).
